weaknesses: The evaluation does not establish statistical reliability. Results appear to be single runs without confidence intervals or significance tests, while many improvements are only 0.001–0.02. Moreover, BBH and MMLU are split from their test sets, leaving only about 10% for evaluation; these small, nonstandard test sets make the reported differences especially vulnerable to split and training variance.

Hyperparameter selection is insufficiently controlled. The token ratio is changed from 70% to 30% for one transfer because it performed best, and generation parameters are tuned separately by task, but no validation sets, search protocol, or separation from the reported evaluation data is described. This leaves substantial risk of test-set tuning.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed contribution. TITOK changes the query generator, sample filter, and token-level objective simultaneously. Missing controls include full-token training on exactly the same selected data, alternative ranking signals such as expert confidence, base loss, entropy or logit divergence, and random-token controls. Source-expert and target-model training on the original data are also absent, so the amount of source knowledge retained cannot be assessed.

The same-backbone Mistral-to-Mistral experiment omits the obvious direct-copy baseline, even though the original LoRA can simply be reused on an identical backbone. KD and TransLoRA also use differently generated or filtered data, weakening the fairness of the headline comparison.

Several technical and reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence. As written, the floor operation in the top-k objective can select zero tokens for one-token classification labels. Tokenizer alignment lacks specified normalization, failure handling, and tie-breaking. Figure 3(a), labeled as average BBH accuracy for Mistral-to-Mistral, plots roughly 0.11–0.12 despite Table 1 reporting 0.397–0.432, and Table 3 inconsistently labels related baselines as KD versus MinED.

The efficiency claim is unsupported: TITOK generates a pool twice the training-set size and evaluates both the base and adapted source model over every response. No wall-clock time, FLOPs, memory, or end-to-end cost comparison is given, so avoiding a trained discriminator does not demonstrate lower overall overhead.

Reproducibility remains limited. Code is only promised after publication; split and run seeds, task-specific sampling parameters, complete label-generation prompts, compute requirements, and whether adapters are trained per subtask or per user are unclear. The text also states that LaMP uses 6,000 training examples while Appendix F sets the source-sized retained set to 200 without adequately explaining the unit.

The novelty is moderate: contrastive adapted-versus-base likelihood ratios combined with selective language-model training and synthetic distillation are a straightforward composition of existing ideas. The empirical evidence is not strong enough to establish that the proposed score specifically measures transferable adapter knowledge.

Headline percentage gains are computed by aggregating heterogeneous accuracy and ROUGE values and reporting relative improvement, which can exaggerate practical impact. The token-selection component itself adds only small gains in much of Table 2.

The privacy discussion is too strong: the method still prompts with raw seed examples and generates from an adapter that may memorize personalized data, yet no leakage or memorization audit supports the claim that raw user information is not exposed. strengths: Addresses a practical problem: transferring task knowledge between otherwise incompatible LoRA backbones.
The token-wise expert-versus-base score is simple, intuitive, and avoids training TransLoRA's discriminator.
Evaluation spans reasoning and generation tasks, four principal transfer settings, and mostly shows consistent improvements over the reported baselines across three seeds.
The paper includes useful component ablations, token-subgroup comparisons, sensitivity analyses, tokenizer-alignment experiments, external-data tests, and runtime measurements.
weaknesses: The central comparison is confounded: TITOK uses source-expert-generated queries, whereas KD and TransLoRA use TransLoRA's target-generated data. Figure 3 shows that query source alone can cause large gains. Comprehensive same-data, matched-budget comparisons against full-token training, random masking, expert-confidence, entropy, and other inexpensive filters are missing.

No separate validation set is described. The token ratio and task-specific generation hyperparameters appear selected using the reported evaluation splits, creating test-set tuning. Generated-query overlap with held-out BBH/MMLU examples is also not checked.

The novelty and theory are overstated. The score is a straightforward realized log-likelihood ratio closely related to prior contrastive decoding and excess-loss token selection. The Neyman-Pearson lemma does not establish that high-scoring tokens are optimal for transfer to a different target model, nor that they necessarily produce larger target gradients.

Several gains over the strongest baseline are small relative to the reported standard deviations, yet there are no paired significance tests or task/user-level confidence intervals. Most ablations use one seed and aggregate across transfer settings, obscuring failures.
The same-backbone settings omit the obvious direct-copy LoRA baseline. The additional MoE/70B results compare only against vanilla on BBH and provide neither competing methods nor uncertainty.

There are material reporting inconsistencies: Table 7 gives the wrong vanilla values for Mistral-to-Llama and News scores inconsistent with other tables; Table 19's target baseline differs from Table 1; Equation 3 calls log probabilities losses; and the stated floor-based top-k rule may select zero tokens for short classification labels.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the claimed public-code URL is blank, while generation parameters, seeds, splits, LoRA target modules, hardware, and many exact prompts are omitted. Claims of no additional overhead and of privacy/bias protection are also stronger than the runtime and ethical evidence support.
